newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's largest unions plan tax reform protest.
newsitem.headline: Germany's largest unions plan tax reform protest.

text.p: Germany's two largest and most powerful unions said on Tuesday they planned to rally their members in protest against the government's plans for a sweeping reform of the tax system.

The IG Metall engineering union and OeTV public services union -- which together represent over five million workers -- said they would gather hundreds of thousands of signatures in a petition protesting against the changes.
The petition would be accompanied by demonstrations at factory gates, in front of hospitals and at other public buildings, the two unions said.

IG Metall leader Klaus Zwickel and OeTV leader Herbert Mai lashed out at two key elements of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's reform proposals -- a 14-point cut in the top income tax rate and plans to end tax relief on weekend, night and holiday pay.

"The federal government's tax reform plans are just like all other reform proposals made by this government recently: the rich will get richer, the poor pick up the tab, and the intended effect is not achieved," Zwickel told reporters.

Germany's ruling parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) met on Monday for a rare "summit" on tax reforms, the opening session in a battle described as Bonn's last chance to whip soaring unemployment.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine met to discuss a coalition plan to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes to boost job-creation after Germany's January unemployment hit 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933.
The two sides made no early breakthrough but agreed to meet again this week.
Zwickel made clear that a major reason for the unions' action would be to support the SPD in the talks.

"Our aim will be to give strength to the SPD's position," he said, adding that one reason for starting the protest action now was to coordinate this with the start of the parliamentary debate on the issue.

The SPD has already made clear its opposition to the planned cut in the top tax rate to 39 from 53 percent and the issue of whether pay supplements should be taxed are central points in its negotiating position.

Mai criticised in particular Waigel's plans to tax supplements paid to workers who work unsocial hours, saying that would hurt groups such as nurses and transport workers who had no option but to work through the night.

"I find it completely incomprehensible that Waigel should seek to tax these," he said, adding that the finance minister had earlier assured the OeTV in writing that this change would not be part of the reform agreement.

Zwickel argued that money returned to higher-earners -- by cutting their taxes -- was unlikely to be channeled into the sort of investment or consumption that the government hoped would emerge to create new jobs in the economy.
"Experience shows that this group of people does not use saved money for consumption but invests it, and it is by no means certain that this is automatically in Germany," he said.

But the unions, which successfully sabotaged recent government attempts to cut back on sick pay, provided no clear new proposals as to how Germany could revamp its tax system to create new jobs while also taking account of their demands.
They also signalled they had no plans to call members out in a full strike over the issue.
"This is not a case for strike, Klaus Zwickel and I agree on that," Mai said.
